title: IRGC Says Supertanker Struck Mine and Exploded Trying to Exit Strait of Hormuz
excerpt: The Revolutionary Guards said the vessel was sailing dark, with navigation systems switched off, through a route Tehran had declared high-risk; the vessel was not identified and the account has not been independently verified.
body:
• Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said on Saturday that a "violating" supertanker exploded after striking naval mines while trying to exit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route, catching fire.
  • The crude-carrying vessel had its navigation and GPS systems switched off, the IRGC said; it was not named, and there is no word on its crew or casualties.
  • The Revolutionary Guards warned of "a horrific fire" for ships ignoring its rules, said enforcement would no longer be limited to the strait, and blamed the US military for rising tensions.
  • The account has not been independently verified. UKMTO separately reported an outbound tanker struck by a projectile inside the strait on Saturday, with its crew safe.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Saturday that an oil supertanker carrying around 2 million barrels of crude struck a naval mine and exploded while attempting to leave the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized southern route, in the latest escalation of a confrontation that has seen more than a dozen commercial ships attacked in and around the waterway since early October.

In a statement published by the IRGC's official outlet Sepah News, the navy said the vessel was sailing with its navigation and GPS systems switched off when it hit the mines, triggering an explosion it said was visible from coastal areas, followed by fire. There was no immediate information about the vessel's identity, its crew or possible casualties, and the claim has not been independently verified.

Context & Background

The statement followed a separate claim a day earlier, when the IRGC navy said its forces had struck the liquefied petroleum gas carrier NV Sunshine as it sought to cross the strait through what Iran described as an illegal southern route, causing fires in the vessel's engine room and propulsion system. Independent confirmation of that account remains elusive, according to maritime reporting.

https://x.com/FaytuksNetwork/status/2108969581754622294

Iran announced on July 12 that it had again closed the Strait of Hormuz following the resumption of US strikes on July 8. Tehran has barred safe passage for vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States since February 28, following what it described as joint strikes on Iranian territory, and has warned that any ship using routes it considers unauthorized or transiting without permission would face action. The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28 that killed more than 3,000 people, according to Tehran; Iran retaliated with attacks that killed Americans and Israelis before a ceasefire was reached in April, and the United States subsequently carried out further strikes amid stalled negotiations. About 20 percent of the world's oil passes through the strait, making any disruption a global energy event.

Impact & Analysis

Separately on Saturday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that an unidentified outbound tanker was struck on its port side by a projectile within the strait, triggering a fire; its crew was reported safe. The two accounts suggest multiple incidents over the weekend, though they may describe the same vessel. Maritime security analysts say the combination of naval mines, small drones and IRGC boarding parties creates an asymmetric threat that conventional naval protection has not neutralized, and charterers are being forced to weigh rerouting against sharply higher war-risk insurance. One industry assessment put the going rate for ship captains willing to accept Hormuz transits at $100,000 a month.

"The fate of every vessel that ignores the rules in the Strait of Hormuz is a horrific fire."

— Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps

The IRGC's warning that actions against vessels using unauthorized routes will no longer be limited to the strait signals a potentially wider operational reach. The Guards attributed responsibility for rising maritime tensions to the US military. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Thursday, in a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, that Iran would not abandon negotiations with the United States even as he accused Washington of attacking during previous rounds of talks.

Diaspora Angle

India imports the bulk of its crude oil, so a disruption in the Strait of Hormuz feeds directly into India's import bill and fuel prices, a number every NRI household with family in India watches closely. Thousands of Indian seafarers also crew the tankers transiting these waters.

What's Next

Whether the IRGC's unnamed vessel is identified and the crew accounted for is the immediate open question; the Guards' account remains unverified. Watch for any US response, further UKMTO incident reports, and whether Tehran acts on its warning to extend enforcement beyond the strait.
